title: Beginner Arabic
summary: Start learning Modern Standard Arabic: the script and its letters, vowels and new sounds, greetings and introductions, pronouns and sentences without "to be", gender and the definite article, numbers and both sets of digits, and everyday words and questions.
audience: Complete beginners, students, travellers and professionals working with Arabic speakers

body.p: Arabic is spoken by hundreds of millions of people across North Africa and the Middle East and is an official language in countries such as Egypt, Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Sudan, Mauritania and Chad, among others. It is the language of the Qur'an and an official language of the United Nations and the African Union.

Modern Standard Arabic (MSA, al-fuṣḥā) is used in writing, news, formal speeches and education throughout the Arab world. Everyday speech uses regional dialects, such as Egyptian, Moroccan (Darija) or Sudanese Arabic, which can differ considerably. This course teaches MSA, understood everywhere, with common greetings.

list: Arabic is written from right to left.
The alphabet has 28 letters, all consonants or long vowels.
Most letters join to the next letter, and change shape depending on whether they are at the start, middle or end of a word, or alone.
Short vowels are usually not written in everyday text; they appear as small marks in learners' texts and the Qur'an.
There are no capital letters.

body.tip: Learn to recognise letters in their joined forms early; real text is almost always joined.

list: Long vowels are written with letters: ا (alif) for ā, و (wāw) for ū, ي (yāʾ) for ī.
Short vowels are marks: fatḥa (a short line above, "a"), kasra (a short line below, "i"), ḍamma (a small wāw-shape above, "u").
Sukūn (a small circle above) shows no vowel; shadda (a small w-shape above) doubles a consonant.
ع (ʿayn): a tightening of the throat, as in عربي ʿarabī (Arabic).
ح (ḥāʾ): a strong, breathy h from the throat, as in حب ḥubb (love).
خ (khāʾ): like ch in Scottish "loch".
غ (ghayn): like a gargled French r.
ق (qāf): a k sound made further back in the throat.
The emphatic letters ص ض ط ظ are pronounced with the tongue pulled back, making nearby vowels sound deeper.

body.p: Transliteration in this course uses common conventions: ʿ for ʿayn, ʾ for the glottal stop hamza, and a line over a vowel for length (ā, ī, ū).

body.tip: Listen to recordings of each letter and copy them aloud; Arabic pronunciation is learned by ear.

list: السلام عليكم (as-salāmu ʿalaykum): peace be upon you, the most common greeting.
وعليكم السلام (wa-ʿalaykum as-salām): and upon you peace, the reply.
مرحبا (marḥaban): hello.
صباح الخير (ṣabāḥ al-khayr): good morning; reply صباح النور (ṣabāḥ an-nūr).
مساء الخير (masāʾ al-khayr): good evening.
كيف حالك؟ (kayfa ḥāluk?): How are you? (ḥāluka to a man, ḥāluki to a woman).
بخير، الحمد لله (bikhayr, al-ḥamdu lillāh): fine, praise be to God.
شكرا (shukran): thank you. عفوا (ʿafwan): you're welcome, excuse me.
من فضلك (min faḍlik): please.
مع السلامة (maʿa as-salāma): goodbye.

body.p: اسمي فاطمة (ismī Fāṭima): my name is Fatima. ما اسمك؟ (mā ismuka / ismuki?): What is your name? (to a man / a woman). أنا من كينيا (anā min Kīnyā): I am from Kenya. تشرفنا (tasharrafnā): pleased to meet you.

body.tip: Arabic often changes endings for male or female listeners; notice who you are speaking to.

body.p: أنا (anā) I; أنتَ (anta) you (man); أنتِ (anti) you (woman); هو (huwa) he; هي (hiya) she; نحن (naḥnu) we; أنتم (antum) you (plural); هم (hum) they.

In the present tense, Arabic usually does not use a verb "to be": أنا طالب (anā ṭālib) means "I am a student"; هي طالبة (hiya ṭāliba) means "she is a student"; البيت كبير (al-bayt kabīr) means "the house is big".

list: Many feminine nouns and adjectives end in ة (tāʾ marbūṭa): طالب ṭālib (male student), طالبة ṭāliba (female student).
The definite article is ال (al-), joined to the word: كتاب kitāb (a book), الكتاب al-kitāb (the book).

Before "sun letters" such as ش, س, ت, د, ر and ن, the l of al- is not pronounced and the next consonant doubles: الشمس ash-shams (the sun). Before "moon letters" it is pronounced: القمر al-qamar (the moon).
Adjectives follow the noun and agree with it: بيت كبير bayt kabīr (a big house).

body.tip: Make your own sentences with a pronoun plus a noun or adjective: أنا سعيد (anā saʿīd), I am happy.

body.p: 1 واحد (wāḥid), 2 اثنان (ithnān), 3 ثلاثة (thalātha), 4 أربعة (arbaʿa), 5 خمسة (khamsa), 6 ستة (sitta), 7 سبعة (sabʿa), 8 ثمانية (thamāniya), 9 تسعة (tisʿa), 10 عشرة (ʿashara). Note the unusual rule that numbers 3 to 10 take the opposite gender form to the noun they count, which learners can practise later.

Many Arab countries in the Middle East use Eastern Arabic numerals: ٠ ١ ٢ ٣ ٤ ٥ ٦ ٧ ٨ ٩ (0 to 9). North African countries mainly use the Western digits 0 to 9, which are themselves called "Arabic numerals" in English. Digits are written left to right even inside right-to-left text: the year 2026 is ٢٠٢٦.

list: كم؟ (kam?): how many?
بكم؟ / بكم هذا؟ (bikam hādhā?): how much is this?
الساعة الثالثة (as-sāʿa ath-thālitha): three o'clock.

body.tip: Read prices and phone numbers on Arabic-language websites to practise recognising Eastern Arabic digits.

list: ما؟ (mā?) / ماذا؟ (mādhā?): what?
من؟ (man?): who?
أين؟ (ayna?): where? أين المسجد؟ (ayna al-masjid?) Where is the mosque?
متى؟ (matā?): when?
لماذا؟ (limādhā?): why?
كيف؟ (kayfa?): how?
هل (hal) turns a statement into a yes/no question: هل أنت طالب؟ (hal anta ṭālib?) Are you a student?

body.p: نعم (naʿam) yes; لا (lā) no; ماء (māʾ) water; خبز (khubz) bread; شاي (shāy) tea; قهوة (qahwa) coffee; بيت (bayt) house; مدرسة (madrasa) school; سوق (sūq) market; كتاب (kitāb) book.
أب (ab) father; أم (umm) mother; أخ (akh) brother; أخت (ukht) sister; عائلة (ʿāʾila) family. Possession is often shown with endings: كتابي (kitābī) my book; بيتك (baytuka) your house.

body.tip: Learn words in useful groups, such as food or family, and use each in a short sentence.
